thread.title: Is It Possible To Have A Bear Market Without A Recession?

author: Rick Pendergraft
title: Is It Possible To Have A Bear Market Without A Recession?
text:
The news from this past week has been fascinating to keep up with. We had earnings warnings from Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Delta Air Lines (NYSE: DAL ), we had the ISM Manufacturing Index fall sharply, and we had an employment report that completely blew past expectations. Modest gains on Monday and Wednesday were offset by a huge selloff on Thursday, and then the employment report and news of potential progress in the trade talks with China propelled stocks sharply higher on Friday.
Based on the labor market, it certainly doesn’t look like we are heading into a recession anytime soon. The Fed has faced a lot of criticism that they have raised rates too fast and by too much, but that certainly isn’t being reflected in the employment reports. Analysts expected job growth of 180K for December and instead we saw nonfarm payrolls grow by 312K.
In addition to the headline number, average hourly earnings increased more than expected, and the average hourly work week increased from November. This is not the backdrop of a lurking recession.
So why is the stock market so jittery?
Today’s Market Resembles the 2000 Market More Than the 2007 Market Most people assume that bear markets and recessions go hand in hand. But that wasn’t the case in the bear market of 2000-2002. By definition, a recession occurs when GDP declines in two or more consecutive quarters. In the time period in question, we saw GDP declines in the first quarter of 2001 and again in the third quarter.
Despite the fact that the U.S. never technically entered a recession in 2000-2002, the stock market dropped dramatically. The S&P dropped almost 50% from the high in September 2000 to the low in October 2002.
Even though the economy didn’t enter into a recession, the unemployment rate was low in 2000 and started rising toward the end of the year. The rate exceeded 4% in January 2001 and then rose above 4.5% in July 2001. It would eventually rise to 6.3% in the summer of 2003.
I mentioned the ISM Manufacturing Index earlier and how it fell in December. The index came in with a reading of 54.1 and that was a sharp decline from the 59.3 reading in November. The good news is that the index remained above 50 because readings above 50 indicate that the economy is growing while readings below 50 indicate that the economy is contracting.
The ISM index did fall below the 50 level back in the 2000-2002 timeframe but not until April 2001. In fact, the ISM index was below 50 in nine out of 10 months from April ’01 through January ’02. Yes, we saw two quarters of GDP decline but didn’t enter a recession.
Another economic indicator that was at similar levels to where we are now or have been in recent months is the consumer confidence index. I have shared the chart below with readers before but felt like it needed to be shared again. Consumer confidence peaked at 144.7 in July ’00 and then started falling.
My studies of the index have led me to conclude that when it hits extreme highs and then falls 10% is when we run into problems with the stock market. The recent high hit 137.9 in October and fell to 128.1 in December. A reading of 124.1 or lower would be a concern from my perspective.
As you can see, there are a number of economic indicators that are at similar levels or behaving in a similar manner to 2000. It will be interesting to see whether the ISM index falls below 50, consumer confidence falls by 10%, and whether or not we start seeing lower GDP numbers in the coming months. The trade war with China isn’t going to help the numbers and neither is the government shutdown.
There are Stock Market Similarities as Well In addition to the economic similarities, there are certain characteristics in the stock market that are similar between 2000 and now. We saw tech stocks drop sharply back in 2000 and the sector was one of the first ones to break major support levels like the 52-week moving average.
We also had major earnings misses in 2000. The first one I remember was Microsoft in April ’00. The company issued an earnings report where revenue fell short of expectations and that triggered a big tech selloff. The Nasdaq plunged almost 5% on April 24, 2000.
The sector managed to stabilize a little and moved sideways from May through September, but then the earnings reports took their toll. I seem to recall numerous companies issuing earnings warnings back then. The tech sector dropped sharply in the fourth quarter that year.
We had companies like Facebook and Netflix miss earnings or revenue numbers this past summer and now we just got the earnings warning from Apple. We saw a big decline in the tech sector in the fourth quarter just like we had in 2000.
Now we have started 2019 with wild swings in the market. The S&P dropped 2.5% on January 3 of this year and bounced back with a gain of 3.43% on January 4.
Believe it or not, 2001 started in a similar manner. The S&P dropped 2.8% on January 2 and then bounced back with a 5% gain on January 3. The S&P turned around and gave all of that 5% gain back on January 4, 5, and at the open on January 8. The index did bounce back and from the close on January 8, 2001 through the high on January 31, it gained 8.4%.
I have pointed out before that the quick rally in January ’01 got stopped at the 104-week moving average and then the S&P fell 21.8% from the January high to the March low.
Do I expect everything to go exactly the same way in 2019? Of course not, but I do think that there are way too many similarities between the two time periods to be ignored.
I stated in an article last week that I expect a rally during the first quarter. That statement was made based on how the market behaved in the first quarter of 2001 and in the first quarter of 2008. After studying those two bear markets more closely, I think the current market environment appears to be more similar to the 2000-2002 market. If that is the case and things continue to play out in a similar fashion, we should see a rally this month and then see the market turn lower again.
I won’t be making investment decisions solely on the past pattern, but you can bet I will be keeping the 2001 market in mind for the next few months.
